narrative:
The model estimated a 61% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, meaning it judged failure more likely than success. On that basis, your law school application was rejected. This is a predictive judgment, not a certainty, but it means the application did not show enough evidence to offset the academic risk the model identified.

The strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure was your LSAT score. At 32, it is below the average of 37.18 among accepted students, so it was the leading reason the model viewed first-time bar failure as more likely. The second strongest factor was your undergraduate GPA: 2.70 versus an accepted-student average of 3.23, which also pushed toward failure. The third most influential factor was your Year 1 class-rank decile. At 6, it matches the accepted-student average, and this factor worked in your favor, pushing toward passing, but it was not strong enough to outweigh the LSAT and GPA signals.

To improve a future application, focus first on raising your LSAT score through structured preparation and a retake. Strengthen your academic record where possible, such as through additional rigorous coursework, and address any explanatory circumstances. Seek admissions advising, then reapply when the evidence more clearly points toward bar success.
